---
title: "Alpha diversity"
format: html
editor: visual
---

Alpha diversity describes the diversity within a single sample. It can be summarized by several measures, such as richness (the number of OTUs), Shannon diversity or Simpson diversity. These measures differ in how much weight they give to rare OTUs compared to abundant ones, and therefore capture different aspects of the community.

This section documents how to rarefy the data before calculating alpha diversity, how to check whether the sequencing depth is sufficient to capture the diversity of the samples using rarefaction and extrapolation curves, and how to compare richness between sites using either rarefied or estimated richness. To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script `010_alpha_diversity.R` and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
library(downloadthis)
library(phyloseq)
library(iNEXT)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)
library(multcompView)
library(dplyr)
load("../../RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
```

To get started, load the OTU table filtered with BLAST (see [BLAST filtering](../otu-tables/filter/BLAST.qmd)). For reproducibility, set seeds (random number generation) at the start of the script to always obtain the same results with rarefaction.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Load the cleaned OTU table from previous scripts
load("RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
```

```{r}
set.seed(100)
```

## Rarefaction

Alpha diversity, and richness in particular, depends strongly on sequencing depth: samples with more reads inevitably contain more OTUs (see [Rarefaction & Normalization](../otu-tables/rare-norm.qmd#sequencing-depth-and-richness)). Before comparing alpha diversity between samples, the data must therefore be standardized. For alpha diversity, rarefaction is recommended [@schloss2024], even when other standardization methods are used for beta diversity: all samples are randomly subsampled to the same number of reads.

How to choose the rarefaction depth, and how many reads and OTUs are lost by rarefying, is explained in [Rarefaction & Normalization](../otu-tables/rare-norm.qmd#choose-the-rarefaction-depth). In this example, we rarefy to 1011 reads: the two samples with fewer reads (120 and 487 reads) are removed.

`phyloseq::rarefy_even_depth()` subsamples all samples to the same depth:

-   `sample.size`: the rarefaction depth. Samples with fewer reads are removed.
-   `replace = FALSE`: subsampling without replacement (like drawing reads out of the sample one at a time).
-   `rngseed`: the seed for the random subsampling, for reproducibility.

OTUs that are no longer present in any sample after subsampling are removed automatically.

```{r}
# Save the chosen rarefaction depth (you can change it, see Exercise 1)
rare_depth <- 1011

# Rarefy all samples to the chosen depth
otu_table_rarefy <- rarefy_even_depth(otu_BLAST_clean, sample.size = rare_depth,
                                      replace = FALSE, rngseed = 100)

# Check the number of samples, reads per sample, and OTUs after rarefaction
nsamples(otu_table_rarefy)
head(sample_sums(otu_table_rarefy))
ntaxa(otu_table_rarefy)
```

Rarefying discards about 75% of the reads, from the samples with a high sequencing depth. An alternative to rarefying is to extrapolate alpha diversity based on the accumulation of OTUs with increasing numbers of reads (see below).

## Interpolation and extrapolation with iNEXT

The R package `iNEXT` [@chao2014; @hsieh2016] draws rarefaction (interpolation) and extrapolation curves, and estimates the diversity each sample would have if it was sequenced completely (asymptotic diversity). `phyloseq` has no equivalent function for this, so we extract the OTU table from the `phyloseq` object and use `iNEXT` directly.

::: callout-note
## Hill numbers

`iNEXT` uses Hill numbers of order *q* [@hill1973; @jost2006]:

-   *q* = 0: species richness (number of OTUs)
-   *q* = 1: Shannon diversity (the exponential of the Shannon entropy)
-   *q* = 2: Simpson diversity (the inverse of the Simpson concentration)

Larger numbers always mean higher diversity. Hill numbers are expressed in "effective number of OTUs": the number of equally abundant OTUs that would give the same diversity. As *q* increases, rare OTUs get less weight. Expressing all three measures in the same unit makes them directly comparable.
:::

### Run iNEXT for each sample

`iNEXT` expects a data frame with OTUs as rows and samples as columns. Use the non-rarefied data: `iNEXT` does its own rarefaction and extrapolation.

```{r}
# Convert the OTU table to a data frame with OTUs as rows
otu_df <- as.data.frame(as(otu_table(otu_BLAST_clean), "matrix"))
if (!taxa_are_rows(otu_BLAST_clean)) otu_df <- as.data.frame(t(otu_df))
```

`iNEXT()` is run on each sample individually:

-   `q`: the orders of the Hill numbers to calculate.
-   `datatype = "abundance"`: the data are read counts per OTU.
-   `endpoint`: the number of reads up to which the curves are drawn. Beyond the library size of a sample, the curve is extrapolated. Extrapolation is only reliable up to about twice the library size of the sample [@chao2014]. Here, we draw the curves up to 10000 reads, slightly more than the largest library size (8506 reads).
-   `knots`: the number of points calculated along each curve. Fewer knots make the calculation faster.

::: callout-warning
## iNEXT takes a long time to run

`iNEXT` calculates the curves and their confidence intervals (by bootstrapping) for each sample and each order *q*. For this dataset, it takes about 10 minutes, but it can take hours for larger or more deeply sequenced datasets. In that case, run it before a long break or overnight. Save the result so that you do not have to run it again, and load it next time instead.
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Run iNEXT for each sample individually (it takes about 10 minutes...)
inext_res <- iNEXT(otu_df, q = c(0, 1, 2), datatype = "abundance",
                   endpoint = 10000, knots = 20)

# Save the iNEXT results, and load them next time instead of running iNEXT
save(inext_res, file = "RData/ITS/inext_res.RData")
# load("RData/ITS/inext_res.RData")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# The iNEXT results are loaded here instead of running iNEXT at every render
load("../../RData/ITS/inext_res.RData")
```

### Plot the curves

The rarefaction (solid lines) and extrapolation (dashed lines) curves of each sample are plotted with one panel per order *q*. The vertical line shows the rarefaction depth.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
p_inext <- ggiNEXT(inext_res, type = 1, facet.var = "Order.q", grey = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rare_depth) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
p_inext
```

If the curves reach a plateau before the rarefaction depth (vertical line), the rarefied data capture the diversity of the samples for this order *q*. If the curves are still increasing at the rarefaction depth, more OTUs would be found with more sequencing, and the rarefied diversity underestimates the diversity of the samples.

Shannon and Simpson diversity (*q* = 1 and *q* = 2) give less weight to rare OTUs and level off around or before the rarefaction depth. Richness (*q* = 0), instead, is still rising steeply at 1011 reads. Richness is very sensitive to rare OTUs and to sequencing depth, and therefore requires the most caution: with the low rarefaction depth of this dataset, the rarefaction curves in [Rarefaction & Normalization](../otu-tables/rare-norm.qmd#rarefaction-curves) also showed that richness is far from a plateau.

### Estimated (asymptotic) diversity

`iNEXT` returns a table with the observed and estimated (asymptotic) diversity of each sample, for each order *q*. For richness (*q* = 0), the estimator is the Chao1 estimator [@chao1984].

```{r}
inext_div <- inext_res$AsyEst
head(inext_div)
```

::: callout-note
## Why we kept singletons

Chao1 estimates the number of undetected OTUs from the number of OTUs that occur only once (singletons) or twice (doubletons) in a sample. This is why we did not remove singletons and rare OTUs during [global filtering](../otu-tables/filter/global.qmd): removing them would remove the information the estimator relies on, and the estimated richness would be underestimated.
:::

## Rarefied vs estimated richness

What is the impact of using the estimated species richness instead of the rarefied species richness?

### Calculate richness

The rarefied richness is calculated with `phyloseq::estimate_richness()`, which calculates several alpha diversity measures at once. `"Observed"` is the number of OTUs in each sample. `estimate_richness()` returns the samples in the same order as the `phyloseq` object, with sample names as row names.

```{r}
# Rarefied richness
SR <- estimate_richness(otu_table_rarefy, measures = "Observed") %>%
  dplyr::rename(SRrare = Observed)
SR$Assemblage <- rownames(SR)

# Estimated richness from iNEXT
SR_est <- inext_div %>%
  filter(Diversity == "Species richness") %>%
  select(Assemblage, Estimator)

# Combine the two tables, keeping only the samples present in both
SR <- inner_join(SR, SR_est, by = "Assemblage")

# Add the sample data (site and land use)
meta <- as(sample_data(otu_table_rarefy), "data.frame")
SR$SiteID <- meta[SR$Assemblage, "SiteID"]
SR$Land_use <- meta[SR$Assemblage, "Land_use"]

head(SR)
```

### Correlation between the two measures

```{r}
# R2 of the linear regression between the two measures
r2 <- summary(lm(Estimator ~ SRrare, data = SR))$r.squared

p_rare_vs_est <- ggplot(SR, aes(x = SRrare, y = Estimator)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(x = "Rarefied richness (number of OTUs)",
       y = "Estimated richness (Chao1)",
       subtitle = paste("R2 =", round(r2, 3))) +
  theme_bw()
p_rare_vs_est
```

Both measures are correlated (R^2^ ≈ 0.39). This is good, because we can use one or the other and obtain a similar general pattern. However, the correlation is only moderate: samples with the same rarefied richness can have very different estimated richness. Does the choice matter for the comparison of richness between sites?

::: callout-tip
## phyloseq alternative

`estimate_richness()` can also calculate Chao1 directly from the non-rarefied data. It uses `vegan::estimateR()`, which is based on the same principle as `iNEXT`. Compare it with the `iNEXT` estimate:

```{r}
#| eval: false
chao1 <- estimate_richness(otu_BLAST_clean, measures = "Chao1")
plot(chao1[SR$Assemblage, "Chao1"], SR$Estimator)
```
:::

## Compare richness between sites

We test if richness differs between sites using an analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by a Tukey test to find which sites differ from each other.

::: callout-warning
## Pseudoreplication

Each site has 9 samples. The land use types are not replicated in the same way (6 oak forests, but only 1 site for each of the other land uses). Therefore, the samples of one site cannot be used as replicates of a land use, as this would be pseudoreplication [@hurlbert1984]. This is why we compare sites here, and colour the plots by land use.
:::

### ANOVA and Tukey test

Fit one ANOVA model for each richness measure.

```{r}
# Rarefied richness
M_rare <- aov(SRrare ~ SiteID, data = SR)
anova(M_rare)

# Estimated richness
M_est <- aov(Estimator ~ SiteID, data = SR)
anova(M_est)
```

Check the assumptions of the ANOVA: the residuals should be normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk test) and the variances equal between groups (Bartlett test). If not, consider a non-parametric test such as the Kruskal-Wallis test (`kruskal.test()`).

```{r}
shapiro.test(residuals(M_rare))
bartlett.test(SRrare ~ SiteID, data = SR)
shapiro.test(residuals(M_est))
bartlett.test(Estimator ~ SiteID, data = SR)
```

The Tukey test compares all pairs of sites. Below are the adjusted p-values of all pairwise comparisons, for both measures.

```{r}
T_rare <- TukeyHSD(M_rare)
T_est <- TukeyHSD(M_est)

tuk <- data.frame(Tuk_SRrare = T_rare$SiteID[, "p adj"],
                  Tuk_Estimator = T_est$SiteID[, "p adj"])
tuk
```

The results of the Tukey test are summarized with a compact letter display: sites that share a letter are not significantly different from each other. We also find the position to write the letters above the boxplots.

```{r}
# Compact letter display
L_rare <- multcompLetters4(M_rare, T_rare)
L_est <- multcompLetters4(M_est, T_est)

letters_df <- data.frame(SiteID = names(L_rare$SiteID$Letters),
                         lettersSRrare = L_rare$SiteID$Letters)
letters_df$lettersEstimator <- L_est$SiteID$Letters[letters_df$SiteID]

# Find the position to write the letters above the boxplots
max_values <- SR %>%
  group_by(SiteID) %>%
  summarise(y_SRrare = max(SRrare) * 1.05, y_Estimator = max(Estimator) * 1.05)

label_data <- inner_join(letters_df, max_values, by = "SiteID")
```

### Plot

```{r}
# Colours for each land use
land_use_col <- c("Conventional agriculture" = "bisque",
                  "Organic agriculture" = "bisque3",
                  "Grassland" = "orange",
                  "Oak" = "darkolivegreen2",
                  "Old Ref" = "darkolivegreen4")

p1 <- ggplot(SR, aes(x = SiteID, y = SRrare)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Land_use), outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(size = 1, width = 0.1, height = 0) +
  geom_text(data = label_data, aes(x = SiteID, y = y_SRrare, label = lettersSRrare)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = land_use_col) +
  labs(y = "Rarefied richness (number of OTUs)", fill = "Land use") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))

p2 <- ggplot(SR, aes(x = SiteID, y = Estimator)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Land_use), outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(size = 1, width = 0.1, height = 0) +
  geom_text(data = label_data, aes(x = SiteID, y = y_Estimator, label = lettersEstimator)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = land_use_col) +
  labs(y = "Estimated richness (Chao1)", fill = "Land use") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
# Plot both side by side
p_richness_sites <- ggarrange(p1, p2, nrow = 1, common.legend = TRUE, legend = "bottom")
p_richness_sites
```

Compare the letters of both plots. Richness differs significantly between sites with both measures (ANOVA p < 0.001), and Oak_20 is the least rich site in both cases. However, the pairwise differences are not the same: with rarefied richness, the grassland stands out as the richest site, whereas with estimated richness it shares this position with the old oak reference forest (Oak_ref), and fewer pairs of sites differ significantly. Be aware that the method chosen will have an impact on the results!

## Exercises

### Exercise 1

Repeat the calculation of richness, but choose another rarefaction depth (change `rare_depth` at the start of the [Rarefaction](#rarefaction) section). Check whether it changes the comparison of richness between sites.

### Exercise 2

Calculate Shannon diversity for each site after rarefying, and test its statistical significance. Discuss the differences between richness and Shannon diversity.

Hints:

-   `estimate_richness(otu_table_rarefy, measures = "Shannon")` returns the Shannon entropy (H'). Use `exp()` to convert it to Shannon diversity (Hill number *q* = 1), in the same unit as richness (number of OTUs).
-   The `"InvSimpson"` measure gives the Simpson diversity (*q* = 2).
-   Reuse the code of the section [Compare richness between sites](#compare-richness-between-sites).
